planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; Mini Pearl performs best with 6+ hours of direct sun but tolerates a few hours of afternoon shade in Gulf South summers without loss of bloom.

directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Mini Pearl, registered by Pauline Henry in 1982, is one of the most widely planted miniature daylilies for its small, clear light-pink, 2.75-inch flowers with a soft green throat held on grassy, narrow-leaved clumps well under 20 inches tall. It is exceptionally floriferous, producing a heavy count of buds per scape and reblooming steadily through summer where heat and moisture allow, which makes it a dependable low-edging or mass-planting daylily rather than a single-specimen accent. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in early spring or immediately after bloom to keep flower counts high.

common_name: Sheffield Pink Chrysanthemum (Hillside Sheffield Pink Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February-March or September-October. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to keep growth compact, since unpinched plants stretch tall and lean under the weight of the fall flower flush.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Sheffield Pink is a Chrysanthemum x rubellum selection closely related to (and often confused with) 'Clara Curtis', but it grows taller and more lax, and its single daisy flowers open a soft apricot-buff in bud before fading to a warm salmon-pink as they mature, giving each cluster a two-toned effect. Like other rubellum hybrids it is a genuinely long-lived garden perennial rather than a disposable florist pot mum, spreading gradually into loose colonies and blooming heavily from mid-October into November in zone 9, after most other perennial color has finished. Stake or grow through peony rings in richer soil, where the taller, willowy stems benefit from support to keep the late-season flower display from flopping.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Chrysanthemum 'Sheffield Pink' Plant Profile
North Carolina State University Extension — Hardy Chrysanthemums for Southern Gardens

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; mimosa is fast-growing and extremely adaptable to poor, dry, or compacted soils but has weak, brittle wood and a short 10-20 year lifespan. CAUTION: mimosa self-seeds prolifically and is listed as invasive in Gulf South and southeastern states — remove seed pods where possible and avoid planting near natural areas.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; established mimosas tolerate drought, heat, salt spray, and poor soils far better than most flowering trees. Mimosa is a fast-growing, umbrella-shaped, deciduous tree valued for its finely divided, fern-like bipinnate foliage and its abundant clusters of fragrant, silky, pink pompom flowers produced from late spring through late summer, which are irresistible to hummingbirds and butterflies. The wood is weak and prone to storm damage, the roots can be aggressive near pavement, and the species is highly susceptible to Fusarium mimosa wilt, which can kill mature trees within a season or two. CAUTION: mimosa is classified as invasive throughout much of the southeastern United States, including the Gulf South, where it escapes cultivation readily along roadsides and disturbed woodland edges from its abundant, long-lived seed; gardeners in this region should weigh its ornamental value against its weedy tendencies and consider deadheading spent flowers before pods form.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Assessment of Non-Native Plants

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Summer Chocolate holds its rich foliage color best with a half-day or more of direct sun and shows some improved resistance to Fusarium wilt over the green species, though it is not immune. CAUTION: like the species, it can self-seed — remove spent seed pods if volunteer seedlings near natural areas are a concern.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Summer Chocolate is a purple-leaved sport of mimosa selected for its deep bronze-chocolate, finely divided, fern-like foliage, which holds its dark color through the heat of summer far better than most other purple-leaved trees and provides a striking, season-long contrast to the pale pink, silky pompom flowers produced from early summer into fall. It is somewhat smaller and more restrained in habit than the straight green species, typically reaching 15-20 feet, and its weak, brittle wood still benefits from a sheltered planting site away from strong winds. Because it is grafted or vegetatively propagated onto known rootstock, Summer Chocolate is more predictable in size and color than seed-grown mimosas, but gardeners in the Gulf South should still watch for and remove volunteer seedlings, as the cultivar remains capable of setting viable seed.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Assessment of Non-Native Plants
North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Golden Shadows Pagoda Dogwood (Variegated Rainbow Pagoda Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Golden Shadows keeps its brightest chartreuse-gold variegation and is least prone to leaf scorch when given morning sun and afternoon shade, unlike the more sun-tolerant green species.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Golden Shadows is a variegated sport of native pagoda dogwood selected for leaves edged in bright golden-yellow around a green center, a combination that brightens through the season and glows in the dappled light of a woodland-edge planting. It retains the species' distinctive tiered, horizontal branching habit — the source of its 'pagoda' name — along with small, flat-topped clusters of white spring flowers and blue-black summer berries relished by songbirds, but it stays noticeably smaller and shrubbier than the green species, usually 8-12 feet tall. Like the species it is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker, so avoid trunk injuries, provide good air circulation, and keep it out of hot, reflected-sun locations where the variegated leaf margins scorch.
sources: Chicagoland Grows / First Editions Plant Introduction Program
